1:
Henry sets the two halves of Joseph's conduct side by side: he fills their sacks, returns their money and sends them away glad, and in the same act lays a further trial on them — our God, he says, thus humbles those whom he loves and loads with benefits. He is careful about the moral of the thing on both sides. Had Benjamin really stolen the cup it would have been the basest ingratitude; had Joseph meant by planting it to take a genuine advantage, it would have been horrid cruelty; but in the issue no harm was done nor designed on either side. Gill gives the practical reasons — to put Benjamin in apparent danger and see how the others would bear it, and to furnish an excuse for keeping him — and Clarke the dramatic one, that the stratagem was contrived to bring them into the highest perplexity so that the discovery, when it came, might have its greatest effect.

Calvin will not let the example pass without a caution. Since God commands us to cultivate simplicity, such stories give no licence to turn aside into indirect and crafty arts; Joseph may have been moved to this course by a special influence of the Spirit. And he presses the harder objection himself: charity is not suspicious, so why should Joseph distrust his brethren and refuse to suppose any good of them until he had put them to the most rigid examination? His answer is that having once found them exceedingly cruel and perfidious, the suspicion was excusable. He also stops over the cup itself, wondering that so great a man drank from silver rather than gold, and offering three explanations — that the age was more moderate than later ones, that the workmanship may have made silver dearer than gold, as secular history often shows, or, most likely, that Joseph kept his household plain to avoid envy.

Gill fills in the incidental detail: the Targum names the steward as Joseph's own eldest son, the city may have been the Zoan of the Scriptures, and the pursuers overtook them easily since laden asses are slow and the steward was mounted. On the cup he reports that the word suggests a large embossed goblet, one rabbi making it a long cup and the Greek rendering it by a Persian name. Keil and Delitzsch narrate the overtaking plainly and note the form of the charge: the theft is not argued but assumed, the men being asked only why they have rewarded evil for good.

The clause about divining is where the commentators separate. Clarke observes that divination by cups has been prevalent among the Asiatics from time immemorial, and that for want of knowing this his predecessors spent a profusion of learned labour trying to save Joseph from the charge of sorcery; his own solution is to take the verb in its general sense of viewing attentively or inquiring. He adds the eastern tradition, whose beginning is lost, of a cup that passed from potentate to potentate and had the property of showing the whole world within it. Calvin takes the practice as real and documented, citing an ancient writer on the Egyptian mysteries and a modern traveller's account of an Arab who told a European party, I have consulted my cup, and found in it that you are of a people our prophet foretold would come under every pretence to spy out the land. Henry and Wesley avoid the question altogether by preferring another rendering of the same words — not that the lord divines by the cup but that he would search thoroughly for it — Henry offering as a further alternative that Joseph might be said to make trial by it whether his guests were honest men.
7:
Gill has one of them answer in the name of the rest, and guesses it was Judah, astonished at a charge for which there seemed no shadow of ground. Calvin explains the boldness of the denial by its source: a good conscience gives men confidence. He also sets out the form of their argument, which runs from the greater to the less. They had brought back of their own accord the money they might have kept with impunity, and that was such a proof of honesty as made it incredible that they should now be blinded by a little gain into bringing on themselves the greatest disgrace and an immediate danger to their lives. Having argued so, they offered to stand by any penalty if the thing were found among them.

The steward does not take them at their word. Keil and Delitzsch note that he modified the sentence they had proposed — the man with whom it was found should be his slave, and the rest should go blameless — and that the modification gave the proceeding an appearance of moderation. Gill makes the same observation from the other side: the steward accepted their terms not to the full extent but in part, so that only the guilty man should serve, which softened what they had themselves offered and left them no ground to object.

The search is described with some care. Gill has them take their sacks down in all haste, as men with clear consciences confident that nothing would be found and eager to have the business over and be on their way; and he notices what the steward did not do — he went to the bottom of every sack after the cup, and took no notice at all of the money lying in the mouth of each, which the narrative never mentions again. Keil and Delitzsch record the order of the examination, from the eldest to the youngest, so that the discovery came last; and they read the whole episode as the decisive test. It would now appear how these men stood in their inmost hearts toward their father's favourite, and whether they were still capable of what they had once done — giving up a brother and bringing their aged father with sorrow to the grave.

Calvin observes that when the cup was found Moses records no complaint from them at all. Gill takes their rending of their clothes for the ordinary token of sorrow and distress, men at their wits' end like distracted persons, and notes that Jacob had done the same, and that the Egyptians among whom they stood practised the like mourning for their dead, as the old historian relates.
14:
Gill notes that Judah is named first because he was the principal spokesman and the man most concerned for Benjamin, having gone surety for him. Keil and Delitzsch describe the return in the same order — Judah leading, the rest following into the house, and the whole company falling down before Joseph to beg for mercy — and give the harshness of his opening as the text has it, that a man such as he would certainly have divined the thing. Gill adds that Joseph put on a stern countenance and spoke as if in great wrath, asking how men who had received such favours could be guilty of an action so base.

Judah's answer is a confession of helplessness rather than of guilt. Gill explains the position exactly: they could not acknowledge a guilt of which they were not conscious, they could not deny a fact proved by the cup in the sack, and though they may well have suspected fraud they dared not say so — which is why they are at a loss how to speak at all. Clarke says no words could more strongly mark confusion and perturbation of mind, and thinks they all believed Benjamin really had stolen the cup, the suspicion being made likelier by his having drunk from that very cup at dinner, since the most honourable mess would have carried the most honourable cup with it. Calvin marks the change of word: they had called themselves servants before out of modesty, and now they hand themselves over as slaves — while still pleading for Benjamin a mitigation of the punishment they had themselves proposed at first, that he might not suffer capitally.

Wesley takes the confession about iniquity found out as referring to what they had done to Joseph years before, for which they supposed God was now reckoning with them, and draws two lessons from it: that even in afflictions where we think ourselves wronged by men we must own that God is righteous and finds out our iniquity, and that we cannot judge what men are by what they have been, since age and experience may make them wiser and better — the men who had sold Joseph would not now abandon Benjamin.

Joseph's sentence keeps the appearance of justice. Gill has him refuse to take them all for the offence of one as a plain injustice. Calvin looks past the appearance to the intention: had Joseph really meant to keep Benjamin and dismiss the others, he would have done his utmost to rend the Church of God with the worst possible dissension; his design was nothing else than to pierce their hearts more deeply.
18:
Henry calls the speech ingenious and pathetic together, and offers three reasons why Judah should be the one to make it — that he may have been a better friend to Benjamin than the rest, that he had bound himself to his father by his word, or that the others chose him as the man of best sense and readiest tongue. Wesley repeats the judgment almost word for word. Henry adds that the address is so natural and so exactly expressive of feeling that we can hardly suppose Moses, writing it long afterwards, to have written it without the special direction of him that made man's mouth. Gill has Judah pluck up a spirit and come near with boldness, yet very politely; Calvin explains the opening request for leave to speak by the length of the story and the danger of seeming familiar with a great man — Judah begins by owning the honour Joseph had received, to show that his boldness came of necessity and not impertinence.

Henry admires the unforced rhetoric. Judah calls Joseph his lord and himself a servant, and puts him on a level with Pharaoh, whose favour is desired and whose anger dreaded; from which Henry draws that religion does not destroy good manners, and that titles of honour given where due are not flattering titles. Clarke reads the comparison as the ordinary Eastern compliment, the monarch being the pattern of all perfection so that the highest honour is to be likened to him, as he in turn is likened to an angel of God; and he notes that Judah speaks because it was on his suretyship that Jacob had let Benjamin go.

Henry marks how Benjamin is presented — a little one, the youngest, not acquainted with the world nor inured to hardship, and the more pitiable because he alone was left of his mother, his brother being dead. There Henry stops to observe that Judah little thought what a tender point he touched; for he knew Joseph had been sold and had reason to believe him living, but the brothers had told their father he was dead so long that they had begun to believe the lie themselves. Gill notices a similar delicacy: Judah suppresses the real reason Joseph had demanded Benjamin, which was to test whether they were spies, and speaks as if the demand had been meant kindly — as, Gill adds, it undoubtedly was. Keil and Delitzsch confirm the point from the idiom, since to set one's eyes upon a man means to show him good-will. Henry finds a third instance in the reporting of their own words: to their father the brothers had said flatly that they would not go down without Benjamin, but Judah softens it to their not being able to go with any expectation of speeding well — from which he concludes that indecent words spoken in haste to superiors should be recalled and amended.

The weight of the plea falls at the end on the father. Henry gathers the strands: the old man's life is bound up in the lad's, so that when he sees the boy is not with them he will faint away and die — and Judah's last word is that he himself could not bear to see the evil that would come upon his father. That, Henry says, is the duty of children, to be tender of their parents' comfort and afraid of whatever may grieve them. Gill puts the same point in the plainer form the brothers had used from the first, that their father simply would not be willing to part with the boy.
